findings.claim: Algorithmic surveillance can convert complex work into crude traces whose decontextualization erodes trust and fairness and shapes compliance, alteration, or avoidance.
limits: One crowdwork platform and self-report design.

findings.claim: Monitoring can worsen psychosocial risk even before a formal adverse decision because pace, privacy, isolation, autonomy, and uncertainty are themselves working conditions.
limits: Association and aggregate evidence; no individual diagnosis.

findings.claim: A score can be descriptively accurate about a trace while being substantively wrong about the work, motive, disability, safety context, or protected activity that produced it.
limits: No named system error is adjudicated.

findings.claim: The receipt must attach context before escalation rather than asking the worker to reconstruct context only after access, pay, duties, or reputation are already constrained.
limits: Proposed estate control, not current universal law.

observations.claim: The 2026 Human Relations study defines decontextualization as algorithms failing to account adequately for broader work context while reducing labor to machine-readable traces.
In that study, algorithmic surveillance was associated with lower trust and fairness and higher privacy concern, which related to compliance, alteration, or avoidance intentions.
limits: Intentions are not actual misconduct or exit.

observations.claim: EU-OSHA reports that over half of workers in environments with automated allocation or monitoring experienced severe time pressure and overload, with substantial isolation, poor communication and reduced autonomy.
The same summary reports stress, depression or anxiety among 31% of workers where digital tools automatically allocate tasks or time and 34% where tools monitor work or behavior.

ICO guidance inventories screenshots, webcams, timekeeping, keystrokes, productivity, internet activity, location and audio as monitoring surfaces and says excessive monitoring can undermine privacy and mental wellbeing.
limits: Guidance under review; no case finding.

observations.claim: EEOC technical assistance recognizes that AI and software tools used to monitor or assess workers can create disability screen-out and accommodation risks.

title: Decontextualization, psychosocial load, and context-bearing review
